items.title: My AI Agent Bought Me A Car
items.summary: Sam Herring ’s first real test of Hermes Agent was a shopping tool that matched clothes to photos of ancient pottery. A few months later, the same agent was checking government auction sites every day until it found him a retired three-wheel parking ticket car, which he now drives around San Francisco. In this episode, recorded at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose, Sam, who works on the RL post-training team at Nous Research, goes from those everyday wins to the question everyone in AI is asking: can agents improve themselves? He explains how Hermes grew from an internal productivity tool into one of the most talked-about open-source agents, and why letting it write its own skills was the moment it clicked for users. He also describes an early version that could design its own RL environment, train on Thinking Machines’ Tinker, and hot-swap the new weights into a model running locally. Sam then breaks down Trace to Environment, an idea he credits to Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro work, and the loop Nous is building around it: find the exact point where an agent fails, cluster those failures by type, synthesize environments that recreate them, and train on them again and again. The second half moves from training to inference. We get into whether reasoning models overthink, why leaning on pretraining knowledge can be a model’s Achilles heel, and why choosing a reasoning effort level may be a temporary quirk. Sam also makes his case for activation steering as an underexplored way to get more out of small models, explains where steering meets interpretability, and describes what true continual learning could look like. items.title: Getting Pharma AI Agents to the Right Answer by Fixing the Data and Semantic Layers - with Richard Knoche of Flatiron Health
items.summary: Pharma is moving toward AI agents, but agents only know the context they are given, so gaps in data and meaning turn into wrong answers at scale. In this episode, Richard Knoche, Head of Data Science and AI at Flatiron Health, explains why a strong data foundation and a well-built semantic layer determine whether AI agents can be trusted with complex real-world data. He walks through how historical human analyses can be used to build and benchmark that semantic layer, why having agents resolve ambiguity before answering improves accuracy and reduces handoffs between teams, and why leaders need centralized data governance and agents that plug into any system rather than siloed, bespoke tools. ​ This episode is sponsored by Flatiron Health ​ Emerj works with a select group of AI vendors to reach Fortune 500 decision makers through research, media, and direct access. items.title: Interview #100 Peter Evans, CEO at Xtract One Technologies
items.summary: Peter Evans, CEO at Xtract One Technologies, breaks down why many AI weapons scanners at school and stadium entrances still measure the wrong things. He explains why most "AI-enabled" detectors rest on the same physics as a walk-through metal detector, why knives and laptops expose the limits of that physics, and why a claim of 3,000 people an hour means little if a weak model sends most of them to a bag check. Peter also dives into how to estimate the weapons a system misses when nobody reports them, who should own the sensitivity dial, and what should have happened before police drew weapons on a teenager after a Maryland AI camera mistook a bag of chips for a gun. Finally, he shares why mandates in California and Georgia are racing ahead of testing standards, what an entrance should never be allowed to know about you, and why a 3D printed gun is still not invisible.
